title: The desk behind the raise
passage: A survey of 2,000 office workers found that people who use standing desks earn 23% more on average than people who don't. Coincidence? We don't think so. A Talloak Pro could be the smartest career move you make this year. Free delivery through Sunday.
cue: A Talloak Pro could be the smartest career move you make this year
explanation: Higher earners may simply work at companies that buy standing desks. The ad treats two things showing up together as proof that the desk raises your pay.

whyNot.fal_post_hoc: The ad doesn't say pay rose after buying a desk; it leaps from two things appearing together to one causing the other.

title: Survey: Breakfast Eaters Get Better Grades
passage: A district survey found that students who reported eating breakfast every day had higher grade averages than those who skipped it. Board member Ted Nolan said the result proves breakfast boosts learning and called for free breakfast in every school.
cue: the result proves breakfast boosts learning
explanation: Students who eat breakfast daily may differ in other ways, like sleep or family routines. A survey showing the two go together doesn't prove breakfast causes the better grades.

whyNot.fal_texas_sharpshooter: Nolan isn't drawing a pattern around scattered data; he reads cause and effect into a single correlation.

passage: Fun stat from our running club: members who wore compression socks finished the spring 10K about four minutes faster on average. I've been skeptical of the hype for years, but numbers are numbers. If you want a PR this fall, get the socks.
cue: If you want a PR this fall, get the socks
explanation: The club's faster runners may be the ones most likely to buy gear like compression socks. Bri jumps from "sock wearers ran faster" to "socks make you faster."

whyNot.fal_post_hoc: No runner improved after putting socks on; Bri compares two groups and assumes the socks explain the gap.

passage:
Gina: Noticed something at the reading night. The kids in Ms. Park's class who have tablets at home read at a higher level.
Luis: Interesting. Nico's been asking for one.
Gina: Then get him one before third grade. Those reading apps must be doing a lot.
cue: Those reading apps must be doing a lot
explanation: Kids with tablets at home may also have more books, time or money around them. Gina assumes the tablets are what cause the higher reading levels.

whyNot.fal_post_hoc: There's no before-and-after here; Gina compares two groups of kids and assumes the tablets explain the difference.

title: Q3 numbers and the office plants
passage: Hi all, fun finding from the Q3 numbers: teams on the floors with plants beat their sales targets by 12 percent on average, while the two floors without plants came in flat. Small change, big payoff. I'd love to put plants on every floor before Q4.
explanation: Different floors house different teams, managers and accounts. Priya treats the link between plants and sales as cause and effect without ruling any of that out.

whyNot.fal_post_hoc: Priya isn't pointing to a before-and-after sequence; she compares floors and assumes the plants explain the gap.

source: Harold · checkout line at Lakeview Hardware
passage: You know what I've noticed? The streets that got the new LED streetlights have more break-ins on the police log than the streets that didn't. Fourth, Pine, Delmar, all of them. Bright lights must make it easier for thieves to see what's worth taking.
cue: Bright lights must make it easier for thieves to see what's worth taking
explanation: The city may have put the new lights on streets that already had more break-ins. Harold assumes the lights cause the crime when the cause could run the other way.

whyNot.fal_texas_sharpshooter: Harold isn't drawing a target around random hits; he sees two things together and assumes one causes the other.

title: Trial Finds Reminder Texts Raise Flu Shot Rates
passage: Researchers randomly assigned 12,000 clinic patients to receive either a reminder text or no message. Those who got texts were 6 percentage points more likely to get a flu shot. Because the groups were assigned by lottery, the authors say the texts likely caused the difference.
cue: Because the groups were assigned by lottery
explanation: Random assignment means the two groups should be alike in every way except the text message, so concluding that the texts made the difference is reasonable.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: This isn't a bare correlation. Randomly assigning who got a text rules out the usual third factors.

title: Checkout test results
passage: Team, the checkout experiment wrapped Friday. Half of all visitors, chosen at random, saw the shorter form; the rest saw the old one. Same weeks, same traffic sources. The short-form group completed 9% more orders, so I'm confident the form itself made the difference.
cue: Half of all visitors, chosen at random, saw the shorter form
explanation: Marcus ran a randomized test over the same weeks with the same traffic, so the form is the main difference between the groups. Inferring cause here is fair.

whyNot.fal_false_cause: Marcus isn't reading cause into a loose correlation; random assignment and matched timing rule out the obvious alternatives.
